deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The heading reads 'Berechnung der Bahn der Vesta, aus den Örtern vom 29 März, 8 April, 18 April'. This is the computation of Vesta's orbit from three observations. Olbers discovered Vesta on 29 March 1807. The page sets up all auxiliary quantities of the three-observation method that Gauss later printed in Theoria Motus (1809), Book II, Sect. I, Arts. 136-141: the great circles through the Earth's heliocentric place and the geocentric place of the planet, and their mutual intersections D, D', D''. Notation below: R, R', R'' are the Earth-Sun distances; A, A', A'' the Earth's heliocentric longitudes; λ, β the planet's geocentric ecliptic longitude and latitude. The next page (log P, log Q, 'Erste/Zweite Hypothese', z, log r', a = 2.3596) uses these constants to solve for z, i.e. r'.

(1) DATA AND EQUATORIAL TO ECLIPTIC CONVERSION. Columns 1-2 hold the observed apparent right ascension α and declination (here called D):
- 29 Mar: α = 184°8'32.6", D = 11°47'29.5"
- 8 Apr: α = 181°56'23.6", D = 12°35'56.0"
- 18 Apr: α = 180°7'39.7", D = 12°58'21.2"
These are compared with an ephemeris on the previous page, which differs from them by up to about 50".
Columns 3-4 are the computed ecliptic longitude λ and latitude β:
- λ = 179°1'53.89", 176°40'55.17", 174°52'31.55"
- β = 12°27'4.47", 12°18'…, 11°56'2.82"
The conversion uses an auxiliary angle M (my reconstruction, verified numerically for 29 March):
- log tan M = log tan D − log sin α: 9.3196401 − 8.8587499 = 0.4608902, so M = 70°54'46.82".
- M + ε = 94°22'36.92", with obliquity ε = 23°27'50.10" (50.00" and 49.89" on the other dates).
- tan λ = tan α · cos(M+ε)/cos M: 8.8598858 + (8.8826237 − 9.5145523 = 9.3680714) = 8.2279572, so λ = 180° − 0°58'6" = 179°1'53.89".
- tan β = sin λ · tan(M+ε), written as sin λ / cot(M+ε): 8.2278952 − 8.8838922 = 9.3440030, so β = 12°27'4.47".
The same scheme is used for the other two dates, e.g. 81°23'15.92" + 23°27'50.00" = 104°51'5.92" and 89°26'44.52" + 23°27'49.89" = 112°54'34.41".

(2) GREAT CIRCLES AB, A'B', A''B''. The Earth's heliocentric longitudes are A = 188°14'0.15", A' = 198°4'33.89", A'' = 207°51'40.97". The differences A − λ are 9°12'6.26" (written 6.36), 21°23'38.72" and 32°59'9.42".
- The inclination γ of each circle to the ecliptic follows from tan γ = tan β / sin(λ − A): γ = 125°54'47.59", γ' = 180° − 30°53'37.15" = 149°6'22.85", γ'' = 180° − 21°13'0.33" = 158°46'59.67". The next page quotes y = 125.54.47.59 and y'' = 158.46.59.67.
- The arc AB = δ follows from cos δ = cos β cos(λ − A), checked by sin δ = sin β / sin γ. For 29 March: 9.9896633 + 9.9943749 = 9.9840382 and 9.3336663 − 9.9084348 = 9.4252315.
- Results: δ = 15°26'20.84", δ' = 24°32'20.89", δ'' = 34°50'51.55".
- Then log R sin δ = 9.4249250, log R' sin δ' = 0.0009658 + 9.6183774 = 9.6193432, and log R'' sin δ'' = 0.0021535 + 9.7569375 = 9.7590910.

(3) INTERSECTIONS D, D', D'' (blocks I, II, III). Each block solves the spherical triangle formed by the ecliptic and two of the circles, using Napier's analogies.
- Base half-arcs: A'A''/2 = 4°53'33.54", AA''/2 = 9°48'50.41", AA'/2 = 4°55'16.87". The half-sums of the angles at the base are (γ'+γ'')/2 = 153°56'41.26", (γ+γ'')/2 = 142°20'53.63", (γ+γ')/2 = 137°30'35.22". The half-differences are (γ''−γ')/2 = 4°50'18.41", (γ''−γ)/2 = 16°26'6.04", (γ'−γ)/2 = 11°35'47.63".
- The half-sums and half-differences of the sides come out as: 24°1'33.32" and 4°24'47.34"; 20°28'46.70" and 8°7'34.88"; 16°8'12.68" and 3°42'30.74".
- Resulting arcs: A'D = 19°36'45.98", A''D = 28°26'20.60"; AD' = 12°21'11.85", A''D' = 28°36'21.64"; AD'' = 12°25'41.94", A'D'' = 19°50'43.42".
- The quantities 5°16'45.11", 17°18'47.64", 12°2'2.50" and the repeated 9.7545209 appear to be check computations; I have not fully decoded them.
- Also on the page: 23°12'2.34" − 19°2'40.00" = 4°9'22.34", and an undecoded line 177°30'14.35" + 149°6'22.85" = 326°36'37.20".

(4) CORRECTION ANGLE σ. The block of products of tangents and cosines (9.3440030 = tan β, 9.3250125 = tan β'', and others), ending in 8.6012292, yields σ = 0°14'47.30". I have not reconstructed this block in detail. It gives δ' − σ = 24°17'33.59", which I denote δ*.

(5) SINE DIFFERENCES. The page lists the arcs and their log sines; the cosines 9.9974179 and 9.9993698 are also given.
- A''D' − δ'' = −6°14'29.91" (labelled A'D' − δ''), log sin = 9.0363169n
- AD' − δ = −3°5'8.99", log sin = 8.7310395n
- A''D − δ'' = −6°24'30.95", log sin = 9.0477345n
- A'D − δ* = −4°40'47.61", log sin = 8.9116302n
- AD'' − δ = −3°0'38.93", log sin = 8.7203614n
- A'D'' − δ* = −4°26'50.17", log sin = 8.8895346n

(6) COEFFICIENTS.
- x = R sin δ / sin(AD' − δ): log x = 0.6938855n. x'' = R'' sin δ'' / sin(A''D' − δ''): log x'' = 0.7227741n.
- log λ = 0.5744448 and log λ'' = 0.2383269 are written beside them; their formula is not reconstructed. They are reused on the next page together with x and x''.
- a = x/x'' = (R sin δ sin(A''D' − δ''))/(R'' sin δ'' sin(AD' − δ)): log a = 9.9711114, a = 0.93564565.
- b = (R' sin δ' sin(A''D − δ''))/(R'' sin δ'' sin(A'D − δ*)): 0.1361043 + 9.8602522 = 9.9963565 = log b. Here 0.1361043 = 9.0477345 − 8.9116302 and 9.8602522 = 9.6193432 − 9.7590910.
- A companion ratio, 9.8308268 = log sin(AD''−δ)/sin(A'D''−δ*), sits beside 0.1944182 = log(R' sin δ'/R sin δ).
- With log cos σ = 9.9999960: b/cos σ = 0.99165477 and b/cos σ − a = 0.05600912, whose log is 8.7482587.
- d = −(b/cos σ − a)/X with log X = 7.9214383 (origin of X not identified on the page): d = −6.711512.
- e = −tan σ / X: log tan σ = 7.6336480 = 7.6336440 (log sin σ) + 0.0000040, and 7.6336480 − 7.9214383 = 9.7122097n = log e.
- c = 1/(2 (R' sin δ')^3 sin σ): 3 × 9.6193432 = 8.8580296; adding log 2 gives 9.1590596; adding log sin σ = 7.6336440 gives 6.7927036; hence log c = 3.2072964.
These feed the TM-type equation c sin ω sin^4 z = sin(z − ω − σ) with r' = R' sin δ' / sin z. On the next page this gives log tan ω = 9.2422845, z = 10°43'6.66" and log r' = 0.3498673.
errors: The 29 March longitude difference 188°14'0.15" − 179°1'53.89" equals 9°12'6.26"; the page appears to read 9°12'6.36". This is a 0.1" slip or misreading with negligible effect; the log sin 9.2038801 actually used agrees better with about 6.2".

R sin δ: if log R really is 9.9996955 (written above sin δ = 9.4252315), the sum is 9.4249270, but 9.4249250 is written. This is a 2e-6 slip in the log, unless the log R entry is misread (9.9996935 would be consistent). The effect on the orbit is negligible.

Napier half-sum/half-difference entries are inconsistent with the final arcs in the hundredths of an arcsecond. Block I gives 24°1'33.32" ± 4°24'47.34", which implies A''D = 28°26'20.66" rather than 28°26'20.60". Block II's 20°28'46.70" ± 8°7'34.88" implies 28°36'21.58" and 12°21'11.82" rather than 21.64" and 11.85". These digits are heavily overwritten, so they may be corrections or misreadings; the effects are ≤0.06".
No substantive methodological error was found. All other checked subtractions (e.g. δ' − σ, A'D − δ*, A'D'' − δ*, δ − AD') and the log combinations for a, b, c, d, e, x, x'' are correct.

results.what: Conversion of observed right ascension/declination to ecliptic longitude/latitude via an auxiliary angle M (tan M = tan D / sin α; tan λ = tan α cos(M+ε)/cos M; tan β = tan(M+ε) sin λ)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical astronomy (18th century and earlier)

results.what: Inclination γ and arc δ of the great circle from the Earth's heliocentric place to the geocentric place (tan γ = tan β / sin(λ−A), cos δ = cos β cos(λ−A))
Intersection arcs A'D, A''D, AD', ... found by Napier's analogies on triangles with base on the ecliptic

Auxiliary constants a = x/x'', b, σ, c = 1/(2(R' sin δ')^3 sin σ), d, e, x, x'', λ, λ'' for the single-unknown equation c sin ω sin^4 z = sin(z−ω−σ), r' = R' sin δ'/sin z, applied to Vesta (March-April 1807)
results.modern_name: Gauss's method of preliminary orbit determination from three observations (Theoria Motus form using intersections D, D', D'')
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss (Ceres 1801; published in Theoria Motus 1809, Arts. 136-141)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working application of Gauss's own, well-documented three-observation orbit method (in its Theoria Motus form) to the newly discovered Vesta in 1807. Gauss's rapid Vesta orbit computation is historically known. The page shows his method in pre-publication working form but contains nothing beyond what is credited to him.

checkable.sympy: import sympy as sp; d2r=lambda d,m,s: sp.pi/180*(d+sp.Rational(m,60)+sp.nsimplify(s)/3600); a=d2r(184,8,32.6); D=d2r(11,47,29.5); e=d2r(23,27,50.10); lam=sp.atan2(sp.sin(a)*sp.cos(e)+sp.tan(D)*sp.sin(e), sp.cos(a)); sp.N(lam*180/sp.pi % 360, 10)
checkable.asserts: Ecliptic longitude of Vesta on 29 March is about 179.0316 deg (179°1'53.89").

checkable.sympy: import sympy as sp; d2r=lambda d,m,s: sp.pi/180*(d+sp.Rational(m,60)+sp.nsimplify(s)/3600); a=d2r(184,8,32.6); D=d2r(11,47,29.5); e=d2r(23,27,50.10); sp.N(sp.asin(sp.sin(D)*sp.cos(e)-sp.cos(D)*sp.sin(e)*sp.sin(a))*180/sp.pi,10)
checkable.asserts: Ecliptic latitude on 29 March is about 12.4512 deg (12°27'4.47").

transcription_corrections: Columns 1-2 are right ascension and declination; columns 3-4 (179°1'53.89", 12°27'4.47", ...) are the derived ecliptic longitude and latitude. The second-row entries read 176°40'55.17" and 12°18'…, with overwritten digits.
'9956879' in the lower block is probably 9.9956879 (leading characteristic omitted).
